L3967: Based upon the general calculation above, there does appear to be a correlation between a higher percentage of trials conducted in North American and the number of melanoma cases recorded during the trial, with the highest incidence density of cases (10.3 per 1000 PYs) found in the tolcapone development program, which utilized the largest percentage of North American subjects (53%). Likewise, differences in melanoma rates between various members of the same medication class also appeared to reflect the percentage of trials in North America.
L3968: Varying rates of non-Caucasian subjects within the development programs was also considered as a possible contributor to the range of melanoma rates. However, the large majority of subjects within all the development programs analyzed were Caucasian: entacapone 98%, tolcapone 97%, pramipexole 96%, and pergolide 98%.140
L3969: 5.5.5 Placebo-Controlled Portions of TEMPO, LARGO and PRESTO
L3970: While most of the melanoma cases within the rasagiline development program were identified during phases of the clinical trials without placebo control, five melanomas were diagnosed during the placebo-controlled portions of the three, Phase III studies. These included:
L3971: 1. TEMPO: Rasagiline arm: 1 melanoma in 121 person-yearsPlacebo arm: 0 melanomas in 63 person-years
2. PRESTO: Rasagiline arm: 3 melanomas in 146 person-yearsPlacebo arm: 0 melanomas in 74 person-years
3. LARGO: Rasagiline arm: 0 melanomas in 77 person-yearsPlacebo arm: 1 melanoma in 74 person-years.
L3972: However, by Poisson analysis the difference in cases between the rasagiline (all doses combined) and placebo study arms was not found to be statistically significant for the three trials combined, or in TEMPO or PRESTO individually.141142143
L3973: 140 The percentage of Caucasian subjects in the ropinirole development program was not located in an initial search of the FDA safety review, and so is not included in the listing given here.
L3974: 141 For TEMPO, PRESTO and LARGO combined: Rasagiline-treated subjects (4 cases/344 person-years), Poisson Exact test – 95% Confidence Interval: 0.003, 0.30, Placebo-treated subjects (1 case/210 person-years): Poisson Exact test – 95% Confidence Interval: 0.0001, 0.23.
L3975: 5.5.6 Logistic Regression
L3976: A logistic regression analysis was considered, in which the contribution of various variables within the rasagiline development program dataset (age, levodopa treatment, duration of rasagiline treatment, geographic location, and other melanoma risk factors) could be assessed for their association with melanoma. However, the number of cases of melanoma was too low to support such modeling.
L3977: 5.6 Conclusions
L3978: The analyses and other considerations of the occurrence of melanoma in the rasagiline development program yielded mixed results. While most aspects were not supportive of a causal relationship between rasagiline treatment and the development of melanomas, other analyses did suggest an increased risk with rasagiline exposure. The specific aspects which were not supportive of a causal association between rasagiline and melanoma included the following:
L3979: 1. The rate of melanomas observed in the rasagiline development program was within the range of rates seen in five other Parkinson's disease therapy programs, and was exceeded by the rate of one of the four (tolcapone).2. Although some cases occurred after more extended rasagiline treatment, the latency between rasagiline treatment and detection of the melanoma was generally too short for biological plausibility (range: 2.5 and 55 months, median 13 months, mean 21 months).3. The rate of melanoma within the rasagiline development trials, and within the other Parkinson's disease therapy development programs for which datasets were submitted, was strongly associated with the study location of the clinical trials. Specifically, studies conducted within North America had higher rates of melanoma than those conducted outside North America.4. There has been a history of case reports associating melanoma with Parkinson's disease and in particular with levodopa treatment. Although the literature on the subject is limited to case reports, my assessment is that the examination of this issue in the literature has suggested that confounding factors, rather than medication, were responsible for the association.5. Melanoma rates are rising rapidly worldwide, making the upper limit of the expected number of cases difficult to ascertain. In addition, the rate of melanoma identification in the rasagiline development program increased considerably following the commencement of dermatologic screening for melanoma, which also complicates the determination of the number of expected cases.
L3980: Elements of data that are suggestive of an elevated risk include the following:
L3981: 142 For TEMPO: Rasagiline-treated subjects: Poisson Exact test - 95% Confidence Interval: 0.0002, 0.05. Placebo-treated subjects: Poisson Exact test - 95% Confidence Interval: 0, 0.06.
L3982: 143 For PRESTO : Rasagiline-treated subjects - 95% Confidence Interval: 0.004, 0.06.; Placebo-treated subjects: Poisson Exact test - 95% Confidence Interval: 0, 0.05
L3983: 1. The number of melanomas within the rasagiline development program was more than would be expected based upon the rate of melanoma in the general population, as reported to SEER. This is true even when the analysis is restricted to invasive melanomas (for which the reporting to SEER is considered more accurate) and possible under-reporting to the SEER database is corrected by a factor of two- and three-fold.2. As compared to the number of melanomas expected by rates within the American Academy of Dermatology screening program, the observed number of melanomas within the rasagiline development program was not more than expected for invasive melanomas, but was more than expected (Incidence Density Ratio: 10.2, 95% Confidence Interval: 3.7, 22.1) for in situ melanomas.
L3984: 5.6.1 Phase IV Randomized Controlled Trial
L3985: While the data accumulated during the rasagiline development program is generally not supportive of a causal association between rasagiline and melanoma, the analysis is limited by the lack of a demographically equivalent, parallel control group. It is therefore recommended that Teva fully address this question through a Phase IV agreement by conducting a randomized controlled trial in rasagiline-exposed and unexposed Parkinson's disease patients to measure melanoma incidence.
L3986: A randomized controlled trial is suggested as this design has the greatest likelihood of producing treatment and control groups that are equivalent except for the exposure of interest. Parkinson's disease patients (both newly diagnosed and those already on levodopa therapy) could be recruited through their outpatient providers. To control for geographic variation in background rates, it is recommended that subjects either be drawn from a single general location, or preferably that equivalent numbers of rasagiline exposed and unexposed subjects be drawn from various geographic areas. Given the much lower risk of melanoma among persons with increased melanin content in their skin, subject recruitment could be restricted to Caucasian subjects only.
L3987: Baseline information for cohort members would include demographic information, information on melanoma risk factors and past diagnosis of skin cancer, as well as information on current and past Parkinson's disease therapies. Subjects would then be monitored through questionnaires (yearly or twice a year) inquiring about interim changes in Parkinson's disease therapies. Active screening for melanoma (once every three months) is recommended, as this will enhance the likelihood of complete melanoma detection and minimize the potential confounder of differing access to medical care. Upon study entry, subjects should also be given basic information on skin cancers and self-examination for suspicious lesions upon study entry.
L3988: 6. Review of Systems
L3989: In the following sections, I review safety data by body system. Teva's presentation divided adverse events by body system, and for consistency I generally utilized Teva's groupings and terminology. However, Teva included psychiatric AEs within the nervous
L3990: system, while I divided psychiatric and nervous system AEs into two separate categories. Teva also included cerebrovascular accidents within the cardiovascular system, whereas I discuss cerebrovascular accidents as part of the nervous system. The sponsor tables and other sources from which the information in the ROS was obtained are listed in Attachments 9.29 of this review.
L3991: In the ROS, I generally note the number of adverse events occurring in 1% or more of rasagiline-treated subjects. Adverse events that occurred in 1% or more of rasagiline-treated subjects and which were more than twice as frequently reported as in the placebo group are emphasized via underlining.
L3992: 6.1 Cardiovascular (CV)
L3993: (Includes general CV Disorders, Heart Rate and Rhythm Disorders, and Myo-, Endo- and Pericardial disorders)
L3994: Deaths: No deaths in rasagiline-treated subjects were specifically classified as CV in nature. However, two subjects whose death was classified as “Sudden Death” may have experienced cardiac arrest. These deaths included a 68 year-old man with severe CAD on autopsy who died suddenly while snorkeling on vacation, and a 77 year-old man with Alzheimer’s disease and a history of heavy smoking who died in his sleep. A third participant classified by the sponsor as cause of death “Unknown” was found dead in an overheated apartment. Her death was speculated to have been due to cardiac arrest precipitated by heat exposure.
L3995: SAEs: No single CV SAE occurred in more than 1% of rasagiline-treated subjects in the two placebo-controlled cohorts. For Cohort 1 (monotherapy), 1.7% of rasagiline-treated subjects and no placebo-treated subjects reported CV SAEs. The only CV SAE affecting more than one rasagiline-treated subject were angina pectoris (rasagiline 1.0%, n=3; placebo n=0). One subject each reported an SAE of atrial fibrillation, cardiac arrest, and myocardial infarction, compared to none in the placebo group.
L3996: In Cohort 2 (levodopa adjunct), CV SAEs were reported by 2.9% of rasagiline 1 mg subjects and 2.3% of placebo subjects. CV SAEs experienced by two or more rasagiline-treated subjects were arrhythmia (rasagiline 0.5%, n=2; placebo n=0), postural hypotension (rasagiline 0.5%, n=2; placebo n=0) and heart failure (rasagiline 0.5%, n=2; placebo 0.8%, n=3).
L3997: Syncope (1.1%, n=15) and angina pectoris (1.2%, n=14) were the only CV SAEs in Cohort 9 (all PD patients exposed to rasagiline) reported by at least 1% of subjects. Notable CV SAEs reported by two or more subjects in Cohort 9 included heart failure (0.4%, n=5), hypertension (0.5%, n=7), myocardial infarction (0.4%, n=6), arrhythmia (0.3%, n=4), arteriosclerosis (0.1%, n=2), atrial fibrillation (0.6%, n=8), coronary artery disorder (0.5%, n=7) and hypotension (0.4%, n=6).
L3998: Discontinuations: In Cohort 1, the only CV AE leading to discontinuation in rasagiline subjects (1 mg/day) was hypertension (0.7%, n=1), compared to none in placebo. For
L3999: Cohort 2, 1.3% of participants in the rasagiline group (n=5), and 0.8% in the placebo group (n=3) discontinued due to CV AEs. One participant each in the rasagiline 1 mg group of Cohort 2 discontinued due to arrhythmia, AV block complete or heart failure, compared to one or none144 for placebo.
L4000: In Cohort 9, no CV AE led to discontinuation in more than 1% of subjects. CV AEs leading to discontinuation in more than one subject were hypertension (0.7%, n=9), postural hypotension (0.5%, n=7), syncope (0.4%, n=5), blood pressure fluctuation (0.1%, n=2), atrial fibrillation (0.1%, n=2) and tachycardia (0.1%, n=1).
L4001: AEs: In Cohort 1, CV AEs occurring in more than 1% of rasagiline-treated subjects were postural hypotension (rasagiline 3.1%, n=9; placebo 4.6%, n=7), hypertension (rasagiline 2.0%, n=6; placebo 4.0%, n=6), angina pectoris (rasagiline 1%, n=3; placebo n=0), and palpitation (rasagiline 1%, n=3; placebo 2%, n=3).
L4002: For Cohort 2, the only CV AEs reported in more than 1% of rasagiline-treated subjects (1 mg/day) were postural hypotension (rasagiline 4.7%, n=18; placebo 1.3%, n=5), hypotension (rasagiline 2.1%, n=8; placebo 1.8%, n=7), hypertension (rasagiline 1.3%, n=5; placebo 2.6%, n=10), and first degree AV block (rasagiline 1.1%, n=4; placebo 0.5%, n=2).
L4003: In Cohort 9, the only CV AEs reported in more than 1% of participants were postural hypotension (7.8%, n=106), syncope (2.4%, n=33), hypotension (1.8%, n=24), angina pectoris (1.5%, n=21), vasodilatation (1.3%, n=18), and palpitation (1.0%, n=14).
L4004: Other Safety Issues: Although the sponsor's ECG evaluation did not reveal important differences in QT prolongation or other ECG abnormalities between the rasagiline and placebo treatment groups in the adjunctive studies, the ECG data collected was inadequate, with significantly limited information for subjects in Cohort 1 and the Phase I/II studies. Vital sign analysis was notable for a higher percentage of rasagiline-treated subjects (13.4%) in the levodopa adjunct cohort experiencing postural hypotension than placebo-treated subjects (8.5%); this is corroborated by the excess of postural hypotension AEs in the rasagiline group compared to the placebo group in Cohort 2.
L4005: Outstanding issues:
L4006: • Teva's analysis of the ECG data from Cohort 1 and the Phase I/II studies is inadequate. Although the data from Cohort 2 are not suggestive of an effect of rasagiline on cardiac repolarization, there is no way to know whether the concomitant levodopa used in Cohort 2 may have had some protective effect on cardiac repolarization. It is therefore important to know what effect rasagiline in monotherapy has on cardiac repolarization.

L4010: 6.2 Gastrointestinal (GI)
L4011: (Includes GI, Hepatic and Biliary System Disorders)
L4012: Deaths: During the rasagiline development program, two rasagiline-treated subjects died from GI-related causes: one from colon carcinoma, and another due to volvulus and megacolon complicated by sepsis, pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism. The latter subject's death is also noted in the Vascular section 6.10. One entacapone-treated subject and no placebo-treated subjects died of GI-related causes.
L4013: SAEs: In Cohort 1 (monotherapy), no GI SAE occurred in more than 1% of rasagiline-treated subjects. The only SAE experienced by more than one subject was colitis (rasagiline n=2, 0.7%; placebo n=0). Constipation, intestinal obstruction, nausea and vomiting were reported as SAEs for one rasagiline-treated subject each, compared to none for placebo.
L4014: For Cohort 2 (levodopa adjunct therapy), SAEs reported by rasagiline-treated subjects were intestinal obstruction (rasagiline 0.5%, n=2; placebo n=0), fecal impaction (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0) and megacolon (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0). The subject experiencing megacolon was the same subject reported in the Deaths section immediately above, and details of his clinical presentation and subsequent death are provided in Attachments 9.2.
L4015: In Cohort 9 (all PD subjects patients exposed to rasagiline), GI SAEs reported by more than one participant were intestinal obstruction (0.4%, n=6), gastrointestinal hemorrhage (0.3%, n=4), dyspepsia (0.2%, n=3), cholecystitis (0.2%, n=3), cholelithiasis (0.2%, n=3), colitis (0.2%, n=3), constipation (0.2%, n=3), gastrointestinal disorder (0.1%, n=2) and gastrointestinal carcinoma (0.3%, n=4). L4050: SAEs: No rasagiline-treated subjects in Cohort 1 (monotherapy) experienced a MS SAE. For Cohort 2 (levodopa adjunct) the only MS SAE occurring in a rasagiline-treated participant was arthritis (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo 0.3%, n=1). For Cohort 9 (all PD subjects exposed to rasagiline), no SAE occurred in more than 1% of subjects. The only SAEs reported for more than one subject in Cohort 9 were joint disorder (0.7%, n=7) arthralgia (0.3%, n=3), arthritis (0.3%, n=3) and rhabdomyolysis (0.2%, n=2).
L4051: Rhabdomyolysis was reported in two subjects receiving rasagiline (0.5 mg) as a levodopa adjunct. Both cases followed a fall and prolonged immobilization. The first subject, who had a history of chronic renal insufficiency, was reported in the initial NDA to have become lethargic, experienced hallucinations, and lost consciousness. Teva later forwarded notes from the site investigator, who suggested that the subject may have become entangled in a blanket and been unable to extricate himself, but did not experience significant changes in mental status. His CPK value was not submitted by the sponsor at the time of the initial NDA. The subject's CPK value was within normal limits (78 IU/L, with normal range of 61 to 224 IU/L) two days following the fall.146 (There were presumably no earlier values.) Teva stated it was unclear how the investigator had reached the diagnosis of rhabdomyolysis.
L4052: The second subject took an excess of trihexphenidyl, developed a suspected drug-induced delirium, fell and was unable to rise for some time. His CPK was 9735 U/L on hospital
L4053: 146 E-mail responses from Teva received on March 31, 2004 and April 12, 2004
L4054: admission. Teva stated that both discontinued the study although they recovered to their baseline.
L4055: Discontinuations: No rasagiline-treated participant in either of the placebo-controlled cohorts (Cohort 1 or 2) discontinued due to a MS AE. In Cohort 9, the only MS AE leading to discontinuation was arthralgia (n=1, 0.1%).
L4056: AEs: For Cohort 1, AEs occurring in more than 1% of rasagiline-treated subjects were arthralgia (rasagiline 7.4%, n=11; placebo 4.0%, n=6), arthritis (rasagiline 2.0 %, n=3; placebo 0.7 %, n=1), leg cramps (rasagiline 1.7%, n=4, placebo 1.3%, n=2) myalgia (rasagiline 1.4%, n=4; placebo 2.0%, n=3) and joint disorder (rasagiline 1.4%, n=4; placebo 0.7%, n=1). For Cohort 2, the only treatment emergent AEs occurring in more than 1% of rasagiline-treated (1 mg/day) subjects were arthralgia (rasagiline 3.2%, n=12; placebo 1.3%, n=5) and tenosynovitis (rasagiline 1.3%, n=5; placebo n=0).
L4057: MS AEs occurring in 1% or more of Cohort 9 members were arthralgia (10.7%, n=146), joint disorder (3.3%, n=35), leg cramps (3.3%, n=45), arthritis (3.1%, n=42), joint disorder (3.3%, n=45), myalgia (1.8%, n=25), myasthenia (1.8%, n=24), tendon disorder (1.2%, n=16) and bursitis (1.1 %, n=15).
L4058: Outstanding Issues: As the two cases of rhabdomyolysis occurred were both confounded by a fall and prolonged immobilization, and one case did not have laboratory confirmation of the diagnosis, we will consider asking the Office of Drug Safety to follow closely for rhabdomyolysis associated with rasagiline treatment in the postmarketing period while holding off on putting rhabdomyolysis in the labeling.
L4059: 6.7 Metabolic and Nutritional (MN)
L4060: Deaths: One rasagiline-treated subject died of a metabolic derangement, although this was an accidental death from carbon monoxide exposure.
L4061: SAEs: No rasagiline-treated participants in Cohort 1 (monotherapy) experienced a MN SAE. For Cohort 2 (levodopa adjunct), the only MN SAE was peripheral edema (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo 0.3%, n=1). For Cohort 9 (all PD patients exposed to rasagiline), dehydration was the only SAE to occur in more than one subject (0.5%, n=6). Alkalosis, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, peripheral edema and weight loss were reported by one subject each.
L4062: Discontinuations: No rasagiline-treated participants in Cohort 1 (monotherapy) discontinued due to a MN AE. For Cohort 2 (levodopa adjunct), the only MN AE leading to discontinuation was peripheral edema (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo 0.3%, n=1). In Cohort 9 (all PD patients exposed to rasagiline), the only MN AE leading to discontinuation of more than one subject was weight loss (0.1%, n=2).
L4063: AEs: For Cohort 1, MN AEs reported in rasagiline-treated subjects, and which were more frequent than in placebo subjects, were BUN increased (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo
L4064: n=0) and hyperlipidemia (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0). In Cohort 2, MN AEs experienced in rasagiline-treated subjects, and which were more frequent than in the placebo group, were weight loss (rasagiline 4.2%, n=16; placebo 1.5%, n=6), weight gain (rasagiline 0.8%, n=3; placebo 0.3%, n=1), gout (rasagiline 0.5%, n=2; placebo n=0), and BUN increased (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), hyperlipidemia (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), hyperphosphatemia (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), hypokalemia (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), and lactic dehydrogenase increased (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0).
L4065: AEs occurring in 1% or more of Cohort 9 members were: peripheral edema (8.4%, n=114), weight loss (4.4%, n=60), hyperglycemia (1.8%, n=25), weight gain (1.5%, n=21) and hypercholesterolemia (1.1%, n=15).
L4066: Laboratory Data: In Cohort 1 there was an increased percentage of subjects in the rasagiline 1 mg group compared to placebo who experienced a baseline to LOV shift from low/normal to high creatinine (4.1% [rasagiline] versus 2% [placebo]) and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) (4.1% [rasagiline] versus 0.7% [placebo]); however, there was no difference between the treatment groups when the PCS thresholds were utilized. Additionally, no excess of a shift from low/normal to high creatinine and BUN were observed in the rasagiline 1 mg group in Cohort 2. Finally, there was no substantial excess of AEs consistent with renal dysfunction observed in rasagiline treated patients compared to placebo patients (see section 6.8 Urological Reproductive).
L4067: 6.8 Urological Reproductive (UR)
L4068: (Includes Urinary System, Reproductive Male, Female)
L4069: Deaths: Two rasagiline-treated subjects died secondary to urologic conditions. One subject died due to carcinoma of the prostate. The second subject died during a hospitalization for a urinary tract infection complicated by pneumonia and cardiopulmonary arrest.
L4070: SAEs: In Cohort 1 (monotherapy), the only urologic SAE experienced by a rasagiline-treated subject was prostatic carcinoma (rasagiline 2 mg 0.7%, n=1; placebo n=0). For Cohort 2 (levodopa adjunct), the following SAEs occurred in one rasagiline-treated subject each, compared to none in the placebo group: anuria, bladder carcinoma, pyelonephritis, and urinary retention. In Cohort 9 (all PD patients exposed to rasagiline), the most common SAE was prostate carcinoma, with eleven events reported among nine subjects (0.7%). The only other UR SAE affecting more than one participant was prostate disorder (0.2%, n=3).
L4071: Discontinuations: In Cohort 1, the only UR AE leading to discontinuation in rasagiline-treated subjects (1 mg/day) was urinary tract infection (rasagiline 1 mg 0.7%, n=1; placebo n=0). For Cohort 2, the following UR AEs lead to discontinuation of one rasagiline-treated subject each (0.3%): anuria (placebo n=0), dysuria (placebo n=0), and urinary tract infection (placebo 0.3%, n=1). In Cohort 9, the only AE leading to discontinuation in more than one subject was urinary tract infection (0.1%, n=2).
L4072: AEs: In Cohort 1, UR AEs occurring in more than one subject receiving rasagiline, and which were more frequent than in placebo, were urinary frequency (rasagiline 1.0%, n=3; placebo n=1, 0.7%), impotence (rasagiline 1.0%, n=3; placebo 0.7%, n=1), albinuria (rasagiline 0.7%, n=2; placebo 0.7%, n=1), prostate specific enzyme increased (rasagiline 0.7%, n=2; placebo n=0), urinary incontinence (rasagiline 0.7%, n=2; placebo 0.7%, n=1), urinary tract infection (rasagiline 0.7%, n=2; placebo 2.6%, n=4) and urinary urgency (rasagiline 0.7%, n=2 placebo n=0).
L4073: For Cohort 2, AEs reported for one or more rasagiline (1 mg/day) subjects, and which were more frequent than in placebo, were urinary urgency (rasagiline 0.5%, n=2; placebo 0.3%, n=1), anuria (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), dysuria ( rasagiline 0.8%, n=3, placebo 0.3%, n=1), kidney pain (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), nocturia (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), vaginal hemorrhage (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), and urogenital anomaly (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0). The urogenital anomaly occurred in a subject experiencing hematuria, who was found to have a renal cortical cyst and renal pelvis ectasia.
L4074: AEs occurring in 1% or more of Cohort 9 members were: urinary tract infection (6.5%, n=88), hematuria (3.9%, n=53), urinary frequency (1.8%, n=24) urinary incontinence (1.5%, n=21), and prostate disorder (1.5%, n=20).
L4075: Other safety issues:
L4076: ▪ One rasagiline-treated subject (LARGO 16429) experienced acute renal failure following aggressive diuresis during a hospitalization for pacemaker implantation. The subject was reported to recover to baseline with hydration.▪ The most frequently detected abnormality on urinalysis was hematuria.▪ Eleven cases of prostate cancer in the rasagiline development program were reported by nine rasagiline-treated subjects (0.7%). In a general comparison to other Parkinson's disease development programs, the risk in the rasagiline development program was somewhat higher than the dopamine agonists and entacapone, but lower than tolcapone, although this was based on a small number of subjects. This higher risk may be explained by the increased prevalence of prostate cancer over time related to improved detection (increased use of PSA).
L4077: 6.9 Skin and Appendages
L4078: Deaths: One rasagiline-treated subject died as a result of metastatic melanoma.
L4079: SAEs: For Cohort 1 (monotherapy), skin and appendage SAEs for rasagiline-treated subjects were reported for skin melanoma (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0), skin carcinoma (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=0) and sweating (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo n=1). In Cohort 2 (levodopa adjunct), skin carcinoma (rasagiline 0.3%, n=1; placebo 0.5%, n=2) and skin melanoma (rasagiline 0.5%, n=2; placebo 0.3%, n=1) were the only SAEs experienced by rasagiline (1 mg) subjects.
L4080: For Cohort 9 (all PD patients exposed to rasagiline), the following skin-related SAEs were reported: skin melanoma (1%, n=15), skin carcinoma (0.4%, n=6), sweating (0.1%, n=1) and herpes zoster (0.1%, n=1). There were no AEs suggestive of toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens Johnson syndrome, or erythema multiforme.
L4081: Discontinuations: No skin-related AEs led to the discontinuation of more than one subject in the two placebo-controlled cohorts. In Cohort 9, the only skin and appendage AEs leading to discontinuation in more than one subject were skin melanoma (0.4%, n=6), rash (0.3%, n=4) and pruritus (0.1%, n=2).
L4082: AEs: In Cohort 1, the only AEs reported in at least 1% of rasagiline-treated subjects were rash (rasagiline 3.1%, n=9; placebo 3.3%, n=5), alopecia (rasagiline 1.7%, n=5; placebo 0.7%, n=1), skin carcinoma (rasagiline 1.4%, n=4; placebo 0.7%, n=1) and contact dermatitis (rasagiline 1.0%, n=3; placebo n=0). For Cohort 2, at least 1% or more of rasagiline-treated subjects experienced the following AEs: rash (rasagiline 2.6%, n=10; placebo 1.5%, n=6), sweating (rasagiline 1.6%, n=6; placebo 0.8%, n=3), benign skin neoplasm (rasagiline 1.6%, n=6; placebo 1.3%, n=5), skin carcinoma (rasagiline 1.3%, n=5; placebo 1.5%, n=6) and skin disorder (rasagiline 1.3%, n=5; placebo 1.5%, n=6).
L4083: AEs occurring in 1% or more of all Parkinson's disease patients exposed to rasagiline (Cohort 9) were rash (6.0%), benign skin neoplasm (4.1%), sweating (2.5%), pruritus (1.1%), alopecia (1.0%) and skin melanoma (1.0%).
L4084: Outstanding Issues:
L4085: ▪ The occurrence of 15 cases of melanoma in rasagiline-treated subjects during the development program was investigated by analysis with various reference populations. This is discussed in Section 5.0 of this review. These analyses yielded mixed results, with some elements of the data suggestive of an elevated risk of melanoma associated with rasagiline use, and other elements not supportive of an association. These mixed results, in combination with the large number of confounding factors (such as age and geographic location) and that most cases were identified in study phases without placebo control, preclude reaching a conclusion on the subject from the data accumulated during the development program. For these reasons the FDA will request that Teva conduct a prospective cohort study to address the issue as part of a Phase IV request.

L4125: 7. Discussion
L4126: Adverse Event Monitoring
L4127: Teva adequately captured and described safety data during the rasagiline development program. The three Phase III trials (TEMPO, LARGO and PRESTO) appeared to have been appropriately designed to capture treatment emergent adverse events and other safety data. The coding of adverse events was generally acceptable, although the FDA did request that the sponsor make several adjustments in how certain classes of adverse events were coded. The most notable of these adjustments was that fall-related verbatim adverse events be coded to both a new preferred term (PT) "FALLs" and, when fall-related verbatim terms included two or more events, to a reasonable PT for the precipitant or resultant verbatim term. Following these revisions, the coding process provided an accurate depiction of rasagiline's adverse event profile.
L4128: Exposure
L4129: The overall number of subjects exposed to rasagiline at any dose (including 1537 Parkinson's disease patients) just exceeded ICH guidelines. The three phase III trials each included a rasagiline 1 mg/day treatment arm, which is the dosage that Teva intends
L4130: to recommend for the treatment of Parkinson's disease. The number of subjects exposed to this indicated dose at six months and one year also met ICH recommendations. As with most NDA safety databases, due to the relatively small number of persons exposed, there was limited power to detect infrequent drug-related events.
L4131: The age distribution of subjects in the different treatment groups within the two placebo-controlled cohorts (monotherapy and levodopa adjunct) was similar. When the age distribution of the two placebo-controlled cohorts were compared to one another, subjects in Cohort 2 were slightly older (mean age 64.2 years) than those in Cohort 1 (mean age 61.3 years) which could be expected given that subjects in Cohort 2 (levodopa adjunct treatment) had more advanced Parkinson's disease. The age mean, median and range were likewise equivalent between treatment groups within the three Phase III trials. When adverse event risk was stratified by age greater or less than 65 years, no meaningful differences in risk were observed.
L4132: For the 1537 Parkinson's disease patients exposed to rasagiline (Cohort 9), there was an overall male predominance (64.4%). A roughly equivalent percentage (~33%) of rasagiline and placebo group subjects in Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 were female. No significant difference in adverse event risk was associated with a particular gender.
L4133: For Cohort 2 (placebo-controlled levodopa adjunct), Teva also stratified data by concomitant medications, including dopamine agonists, amantadine, entacapone and antidepressants. The use of the latter (antidepressants) was significantly restricted by the study protocol, due to serious adverse events associated with concomitant use with other MAO inhibitors. The most notable finding upon stratification was that rash (n= 10), skin disorders (n=5), tenosynovitis (n=5) and extrapyramidal syndrome (n= 10) were reported in the rasagiline treatment group only in participants receiving concomitant dopamine agonists. In addition, hallucinations and peripheral edema were seen primarily with combined dopamine agonist and rasagiline treatment.
L4134: There were no cases of pregnancy or rasagiline overdose in patients receiving rasagiline during the development program.
L4135: Deaths
L4136: A total of twenty-one rasagiline-treated subjects, five entacapone-treated subjects and six placebo subjects died during the rasagiline development program. The reported causes of death were those expected in an older population. Six rasagiline-treated subjects, compared to no placebo or entacapone-treated subjects, died of cerebrovascular accidents. However, rates of non-fatal cerebrovascular accidents were similar in the two placebo-controlled cohorts. The rasagiline development database included none of the following causes of death: acute hepatic failure, acute renal failure, serious skin reactions, rhabdomyolysis, pancreatitis or hematological dyscrasias.
L4137: Serious Adverse Events (SAEs)
L4138: In general, rasagiline and placebo subjects had similar SAE risks. No specific SAEs were reported for more than 2% of participants in Cohort 9 (all Parkinson's disease patients
L4139: exposed to rasagiline). SAEs reported by at least 1% of Cohort 9 subjects were accidental injury (1.9%), skin melanoma (1%) and angina pectoris (1%). In the primary data trials, there were no SAEs of liver failure, acute renal failure, aplastic anemia, serious skin reactions, or pancreatitis. Two SAEs of rhabdomyolysis were reported in ongoing studies, both following a fall and prolonged immobilization. One case lacked laboratory values (creatinine phosphokinase) confirming rhabdomyolysis.
L4140: SAE: Melanoma
L4141: Sixteen cases of melanoma were diagnosed among fifteen rasagiline-treated subjects, and one placebo-treated subject.150 An additional three melanomas were identified prior to treatment initiation. A number of factors complicated the analysis of melanoma within the rasagiline development program. The most significant of these was that most of the cases were diagnosed in extension studies without parallel controls, and that the majority (14 of 20) were identified following the implementation of active skin examinations to screen for melanomas in all rasagiline trials. Other confounding factors include the presence of concomitant Parkinson's disease and other medications (especially levodopa), the variable melanoma risk factors among patients, the different background rates for the geographic locations of the study sites, and the rapidly increasing rates of melanoma worldwide.
L4142: When the number of cases of invasive melanoma (seven cases) in North American rasagiline-treated subjects was compared to the number of invasive melanomas expected by age-adjusted rates with the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) registry of the U.S. National Cancer Institute, the number of cases observed was significantly higher than expected. This remained true even when the number of cases expected by SEER rates was tripled to adjust for any potential under-reporting (Incidence Density Ratio: 3.0, 95% CI 1.3, 5.8).
L4143: To address the effect of the active screening for melanoma on the number of melanoma cases uncovered, comparison was also made with another population undergoing melanoma screening through the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) skin cancer screening program. Although the number of invasive melanomas did not differ significantly from those expected by age-adjusted rates from the AAD screening program (Incidence Density Ratio: 2.6, 95% Confidence Interval: 0.72, 6.74), the number of in situ melanomas was significantly increased (Incidence Density Ratio: 10.2, 95% Confidence Interval: 3.7, 22.1).
L4144: The rate of melanomas within the rasagiline development program fell within the range of rates for five other Parkinson's disease therapy programs. It was exceeded by melanoma rate within in the tolcapone development program.
L4145: While some analyses and other considerations of the data accumulated during the rasagiline development program are not supportive of a causal association between rasagiline and melanoma, others do suggest an elevated risk. However, these analyses are limited by the lack of a parallel control group with comparable demographics and
L4146: 150 One rasagiline-treated subjects experienced two melanomas.
L4147: Parkinson's disease history. It is therefore recommended that, as part of a Phase IV commitment, Teva conduct a randomized controlled trial to assess melanoma rates in Parkinson's disease patients who are exposed or not exposed to rasagiline.
L4148: Potential SAE: Tyramine Reaction
L4149: The co-administration of MAO inhibitors and tyramine (which is contained in a variety of foods such as aged cheese and red wine) may result in a hypertensive crisis (also known as a "cheese effect.") The sponsor studies specifically investigating the potential for hypertensive crisis resulting from interaction of rasagiline with tyramine administration is addressed by Dr. Len Kapcala in his review.
L4150: Safety data was generally not suggestive of the presence of tyramine reactions with the dosages of rasagiline used in the Phase III studies. Specifically, no deaths were attributed to hypertensive reactions. In the placebo-controlled cohorts, no excess of discontinuations due to hypertension was seen among the rasagiline-treated subjects compared to placebo-treated subjects. Vital sign monitoring likewise did not register hypertension more frequently in the rasagiline-treated subjects. In Cohort 9, hypertension was reported as a serious adverse event in only 0.5% of subjects (n=7).
L4151: A possible exception to this lack of evidence for tyramine reactions is a previously normotensive151 Phase I/II subject who experienced an unexplained hypertensive crisis that resulted in her discontinuation from the study.152 No mention was made of the tyramine content of the subject's recent diet in the study report or in the case report form, and a tyramine reaction cannot be excluded.
L4152: Discontinuations
L4153: Overall, 9.4% of rasagiline-treated subjects discontinued the development program early due to adverse event. In the placebo-controlled monotherapy cohort, the rate of discontinuation was higher in rasagiline-treated subjects (7.8/100 PYs) than in placebo subjects (1.5/100 PYs). The most frequently reported AE leading to discontinuation in rasagiline subjects was hallucinations (1.3% [n=2] rasagiline 1 mg; 0% placebo). In the placebo-controlled levodopa adjunct cohort, rasagiline subjects (11/100 PYs) and placebo subjects (13/100 PYs) discontinued early due to AE at a similar rate. AEs reported by more than one discontinuing rasagiline-treated subject, and which were more frequent than in placebo subjects, were hallucinations, postural hypotension, abdominal pain and dyspnea. None of these adverse events were more than twice as common in the rasagiline group as the placebo group. In Cohort 9 (all Parkinson's disease patients exposed to rasagiline), the only AE leading to early discontinuation in 1% or more of subjects was hallucinations (1%).
L4154: The sponsor stated that in approximately 7% of discontinuations they were unable to attribute the discontinuation to a particular AE. In such cases they did not include the AE data for that subject in the data tables for discontinuations, although they did discuss these discontinuing subjects in the corresponding text sections of the NDA. It is
L4155: 151 This subject was normotensive during her prior study monitoring before the hypertensive episode.
L4156: 152 Information on this subject (TVP-1012/111 #808) is included on page 36 of this review.
L4157: recommended that the sponsor should take additional measures to identify the AEs associated with discontinuation. This may include evaluating a listing of all AEs reported by discontinuing subjects along with the dates of their AEs and discontinuation.
L4158: Adverse Events
L4159: Following the re-coding described above, the most common adverse events (defined by the sponsor as those occurring in 2% or more of the rasagiline 1 mg group and numerically at least twice as frequent than in the placebo group) for rasagiline monotherapy were153 flu syndrome, depression, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, fever, malaise, neck pain, neoplasm, arthritis, vertigo, ecchymosis, gastroenteritis, and infection.
L4160: The most common adverse events for rasagiline as levodopa adjunct were postural hypotension, accidental injury, constipation, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting, dystonia, anorexia and abnormal dreams.
L4161: There is a substantial excess of flu-syndrome, arthralgia and fever in rasagiline-treated subjects compared to placebo, most notably in the rasagiline monotherapy cohort. In cohort 1, 4.7%154 of rasagiline-treated subjects reported flu syndrome, compared to 0.7% in placebo-treated subjects: a 6.7-fold excess in the rasagiline treatment group. Within the NDA the sponsor does not provide analysis or commentary on this potential safety signal beyond describing it. The sponsor should present additional analysis exploring the nature of this potential syndrome. These analyses may include the following: creation of a case definition, reassessment of verbatim adverse events to ascertain which meet the case definition, time to onset, trends in associations with other adverse events, concomitant medication (especially amantadine) and examination of these adverse events over time.
L4162: Vital Signs and Laboratory Data
L4163: With the exception of postural hypotension, no important trends in the vital sign or laboratory data was observed in rasagiline-treated subjects compared to placebo-treated subjects. Postural hypotension was observed in a higher percentage of rasagiline-treated subjects than placebo subjects, especially in the levodopa adjunct cohort (rasagiline 3.2%, placebo 1.3%).
L4164: ECG
L4165: The data presented for rasagiline monotherapy (Cohort 1) was limited to the point that additional analyses are necessary in order to reach conclusions on the effect of rasagiline monotherapy on ECG parameters, including QTc interval. The ECG data from Phase I/II studies was also lacking.
L4166: 153 The most common AEs for both rasagiline monotherapy and rasagiline as levodopa adjunct given in this section of the review are listed in order of descending percentage of rasagiline-treated subjects.
L4167: 154 The 4.7% flu syndrome in rasagiline-treated subjects represents the percent following the FDA-requested revision of the coding of certain verbatim terms, and was submitted with the 120 Day Safety Update. In the initial NDA submission, 6.0% of rasagiline-treated Cohort 1 subjects were reported flu syndrome, but a number of these were cases of gastroenteritis inappropriately classified as flu from the verbatim term “stomach flu.”
L4168: The sponsor states that because ECG analysis in the Cohort 1 study TEMPO consisted solely of classifying ECGs as normal or abnormal (without collecting data on the nature of the abnormality or ECG intervals), additional data is not immediately available. It is presumed that the sponsor has retained the original ECG tracings from TEMPO, and it is recommended that these be re-read in a method similar to the sponsor analysis of ECG data for the levodopa adjunct studies. This may include having the ECGs assessed by a centralized facility and more detailed assessment of the QT interval.
L4169: However, Teva's more detailed analyses of ECG data for the two levodopa adjunct studies did not suggest rasagiline-related QT prolongation or other cardiac abnormalities.
L4170: Recommendations for the Proposed Labeling
L4171: It is recommended that the following statement regarding the occurrence of melanoma be included in the _____ the labeling:
L4172: Melanoma
L4173: This reviewer requested that some preferred terms within the initially submitted AE Coding Dictionary be re-coded. As a result of this re-coding there was some shifting of preferred terms meeting or not meeting criteria for "common" and "most common" AEs. Specifically, for the rasagiline monotherapy placebo-controlled cohort, the new preferred term "Falls" meets the criteria for common AEs, while ecchymosis, gastroenteritis, and
L4174: infection would meet criteria for “most common.” In the placebo-controlled rasagiline as levodopa adjunct cohort, ecchymosis, falls and colds were classified as common AEs, while accidental injury was reclassified from “common” to “most common” and arthralgia from “most common” to “common.” The tables of treatment emergent AEs in the proposed labeling should be revised to reflect these changes.
L4175: There was a significantly higher rate of AE reporting in the levodopa adjunct North American study PRESTO (in which 90% of subjects reported AEs) than in the Non-North American study LARGO (in which 50% of subjects reported AEs). Although this discrepancy in AEs was somewhat less when only serious adverse events were compared, it nevertheless remained. The sponsor suggests these differences may be due to cultural variations, however it would seem that serious adverse events should not greatly influenced by potential cultural differences among study populations.
L4176: Given this substantial difference, it is recommended that in the labeling the levodopa adjunct safety data be restricted to that from the North American study PRESTO only, and not be presented as pooled data with LARGO.
L4177: Postural hypotension was a common adverse event, especially when rasagiline was used as an adjunct to levodopa. A statement noting this should be made prominent within the labeling.
L4178: In the proposed labeling Teva notes that significant adverse events have been reported with the use of MAO inhibitors and various concomitant medications. In contrast to the selegiline labeling, the rasagiline proposed labeling does not state specifically what these events were. More detailed information on the nature of the significant adverse events referred to in the rasagiline proposed labeling should be provided.
L4179: The sponsor statements regarding concomitant use of antidepressants and rasagiline during the development program should specifically acknowledge the restrictions on antidepressant usage within the trials and the exact number of subjects to whom rasagiline and antidepressants were co-administered.
L4180: Although overdose has not yet been observed with rasagiline, based upon experience with other selective MAO inhibitors more specific information on the expected symptoms and general treatment should be provided

The participant began radiotherapy. Three months later a surgical excision of a recurrent melanoma on his forehead was
L4246: performed. The participant terminated from the study in — (approximately study drug day 673), and subsequently died of progressive metastatic melanoma.

The patient terminated this phase of the study early - at Week 4 - and started the active-treatment phase, due to a need for additional dopaminergic therapy. His leukocyte count returned to normal eight weeks later, on active-treatment, and declined again at the end of the active-treatment phase of the study. Six weeks after discontinuing treatment with the study drug (week 58) the patient's leukocyte count remained below range. Teva notes that fluctuations in laboratory results occurred prior to exposure to the study drug (from screening to baseline during a six-day interval) and on active-treatment.

L4401: 9.26 Calculations of Melanoma Rates in other Parkinson's Disease Therapy Trials
L4402: Melanoma Cases:
L4403: For controlled trials and extensions, both the summary and the patient files were checked for cases of melanoma (variable names checked include: MRI, MI, MPC, MAC, RIDX, RANDX, DDATE, DD30 and EXTDX)
L4404: Person-Years:
L4405: Person-years for the controlled trial data was obtained by subtracting the date of the first dose of randomized treatment (variable name: FDRAN) from date of last randomized treatment (variable name: LDRAN) for each of the participants, and then summing the results.
L4406: Person-years for the extension trials were calculated by subtracting the date of the first dose of extension treatment (variable name: FDEX) from the date of the last dose of extension treatment (variable name: LDEX) for each of the subjects in the extension trial patient file, and summing the results (variable name: PerYears)

L4450: MEMORANDUM
L4451: DATE: July 1, 2004FROM: Russell Katz, M.D.DirectorDivision of Neuropharmacological Drug Products/HFD-120TO: File, NDA 21-641SUBJECT: Recommendation for action on NDA 21-641, for the use of Agilect (rasagiline mesylate) in patients with Parkinson's Disease
L4452: NDA 21-641, for the use of Agilect (rasagiline mesylate), a presumably selective MAO-B inhibitor, in patients with Parkinson's Disease (PD), was submitted by Teva Neuroscience, Inc., on 9/5/03. The application contains the results of three randomized controlled trials, one in patients recently diagnosed not receiving concomitant L-dopa (TEMPO), and two in patients with late PD experiencing "Off" episodes (PRESTO, LARGO). In addition, safety data and the requisite pre-clinical, CMC, and clinical pharmacology data have been submitted.
L4453: The application has been reviewed by Dr. Len Kapcala, medical officer, neurology team (review dated 6/25/04), Dr. Lisa Jones, medical officer, safety team, Dr. Judy Racoosin, safety team leader (memo dated 6/25/04), Dr. Sharon Yan, statistician (review dated 6/2/04), Dr. Andre Jackson, Office of Clinical Pharmacology and Biopharmaceutics (review dated 5/13/04), Dr. William Timmer, chemist (review dated 5/14/04), Dr. Paul Roney, pharmacologist, Dr. Lois Freed, pharmacology team leader, Dr. Tristan Massie, statistician (animal carcinogenicity; review dated 2/9/04), Carol Holquist, Division of Medication Errors and Technical Support (review dated 1/21/04), Dr. Ni Khin, Division of Scientific Investigations (review dated 4/8/04), and Dr. John Feeney, Neurology Team Leader (memo dated 6/25/04). The review team recommends that the application be considered Approvable. I will briefly review the relevant data, and offer the division's recommendations for action on the application.
L4454: EFFICACY
L4455: As noted above, the sponsor has submitted the results of three controlled trials in patients with PD. I will briefly describe the results of these trials.
L4456: TEMPO
L4457: This was a randomized, parallel group double-blind trial in which patients with early PD (Modified Hoehn and Yahr Score of less than or equal to 3) who had not been treated with levodopa or dopamine agonists for at least 6 weeks prior to their enrollment into the study were randomized to receive either rasagiline 1
L4458: mg/day, 2 mg/day, or placebo. The study was 26 weeks in duration, and was performed in 28 US centers and 4 Canadian centers. The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in the total UPDRS score (consisting of measures of ADL, Motor Function, and Mentation). Patients were evaluated at baseline and Weeks 4, 8, 14, 20, and 26. Secondary outcomes included scores on the individual UPDRS sub-scales, Hoehn and Yahr Stage, and Schwab and England ADL. L4467: LARGO
L4468: This was a randomized, parallel group, double blind trial in patients with late-stage PD who were receiving levodopa and a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor and who were experiencing "Off" episodes. In this trial, patients were randomized to receive either rasagiline 1 mg, entacapone 200 mg with each dose of l-dopa, or placebo. This study was 18 weeks in duration (a 6 week l-dopa dose adjustment phase followed by a 12 week l-dopa dose maintenance phase), and the primary outcome was the change from baseline in the total daily "Off" time (as recorded by patients in diaries).
L4469: Secondary outcomes (to be analyzed sequentially in the following order) were:
L4470: Global Improvement (7 point scale, centered at 0=No Change)
    Change From Baseline in UPDRS-ADL during the "Off" state
    Change From Baseline in UPDRS-Motor Score during the "On" state
L4471: This study was performed in Israel, Argentina, and Europe.

L4488: Demographic Subgroups
L4489: According to Dr. Yan, results did not differ between men and women and patients above and below 65 year old, with one possible exception.
L4490: In the PRESTO study, on the primary outcome measure (total daily "Off" time), at the 0.5 mg dose, men (N=295) had a -1.49 hour change from baseline (p=.02 compared to placebo) and women (N=156) had a -1.12 hour change from baseline (p=.67 compared to placebo).
L4491: SAFETY
L4492: A total of 1537 subjects/patients were exposed to at least one dose of rasagiline during development. A total of 1028 patients have been exposed for at least 6 months, and 674 patients have been exposed for at least one year.
L4493: The sponsor has divided the patients into various safety cohorts. Cohort 1 consists of placebo controlled monotherapy studies (2 studies, TEMPO, 26 weeks, and TV-1012/231, 10 weeks), Cohort 2 consists of placebo controlled adjunctive PD studies (PRESTO, LARGO), and Cohort 9 consists of all PD patients treated with rasagiline (Cohorts 3-8 consist of various other cohorts derived from the various studies; see Dr. Jones's review, pages 23-24 for their definitions).
L4494: In Cohort 1, the median duration of exposure for each of the dose groups (1 mg and 2 mg/day) was about 180 days (149 and 146 patients, respectively). In Cohort 2, the median duration of exposure to rasagiline 1 mg/day was 129 days (a total of 380 patients). About 54% received this treatment for between 18-26 weeks, with another 17% exposed for between 26-30 weeks. In Cohort 9, a total
L4495: of 1360 patients were exposed (see Dr. Jones's Table 9, page 27 for the distribution of patients by dose).
L4496: Deaths in PD Patients (Cohort 9)
L4497: A total of 32 patients in Cohort 9 died; 21 treated with rasagiline. Six rasagiline patients died of CVAs (one CVA death in each of the entacapone and placebo groups), 4 of cancer, 2 of pneumonia, 3 were "sudden" death, and 3 due to unknown causes (the other 4 were clearly not drug related). The deaths were not obviously drug related. No deaths occurred in Cohort 1, and 4 rasagiline and 4 placebo patients died in Cohort 2 (in Cohort 2, 2 rasagiline patients died in PRESTO; 1 in each dose group, both of CVAs; no placebo patients died in PRESTO).
L4498: Serious Adverse Events
L4499: A total of 5% of rasagiline patients in Cohort 1 experienced an SAE (4% at 1 mg, 6% at 2 mg) compared to 2.6% of placebo patients. In the 1 mg group, 4/6 patients with SAEs had cardiac related events and in the 2 mg group, the largest number of SAEs in any one body system was 4/9 patients with an SAE in the category Body as a Whole.
L4500: In Cohort 2, 8% of rasagiline and placebo patients experienced an SAE.
L4501: In Cohort 9, 14 patients reported accidental injury, and 14 patients reported angina. A total of 16 patients experience syncope, but, as Dr. Jones points out, these cases generally occurred after prolonged exposure to the drug.
L4502: Discontinuations
L4503: In Cohort 1, 5 rasagiline 1 mg patients, 2 rasagiline 2 mg patients, and one placebo patient discontinued treatment due to an adverse event. Only hallucinations occurred in more than one patient (3 in the 1 mg group). In Cohort 2, 4.2% of rasagiline and 4.9% of placebo patients discontinued for an adverse event. In Cohort 9, about 10% of patients discontinued secondary to an ADR. Nervous system events accounted for 4% of the discontinuations, then about 3% for CV events, and 2% for GI events.
L4504: In all controlled trials, 6 rasagiline and one placebo patient discontinued due to hallucinations. In Cohort 9, 14 patients discontinued due to hallucinations.

L4518: Tyramine studies

L4548: The data shown indicate that there is a high inter- and probably also intra-individual variability in the tyramine plasma concentrations in each treatment group and also at each tyramine dose level. L4564: No formal statistical analysis was done on pharmacokinetic data. Due to the small number of subjects under TVP-1012 (n = 6 per dose group) and under the different tyramine doses only descriptive statistics were performed and no hypothesis testing was done.
L4565: Safety Evaluations (Adverse Events, Physical Examinations, ECGs, Blood Tests, Vital Signs)
L4566: An analysis of the adverse events (AEs) clearly showed that the main AEs were from cardiovascular system origin and within this system palpitation was the most frequently reported AE. It appears that there were no differences in this AE between the different treatment groups (Placebo, TVP-1012 or selegiline), but that the AEs are more related to the dose of tyramine. The other AEs were rare and occurred in few subjects only. A relationship of the AEs to the study drug was difficult to establish, however, in the opinion of the investigator a relationship between AEs and administration of the study medications could not be excluded in most of the events. The intensity of the AEs was generally mild or moderate and never severe.
L4567: There was one serious AE (SAE) in subject 616. On day 9 of period 1 this subject developed a paranoid reaction. The subject was hospitalized in psychiatric unit for 3 weeks. This subject has only received placebo and a dose of 50 mg tyramine. This subject did not have any related medical history. There were no deaths, or other clinically relevant events observed during this study.
L4568: Physical examinations, performed at screening, during the study and at the end-of-study examination revealed no clinically relevant abnormalities.
L4569: Generally all ECG recordings gave normal results. Few subjects, however, showed minor deviations from normal ranges being of no clinical relevance and these minor deviations were presented in a listing.
L4570: Generally, analyses of hematological and biochemical/clinical chemistry parameters gave normal results. Few subjects, however, showed minor deviations from normality and were not considered by the sponsor to be of clinical relevance.
L4571: All subjects presented normal urinalysis examination results. The tests for screening for drugs of abuse gave also negative results in all subjects.
L4572: Descriptive statistics of hemodynamic parameters, such as supine pulse rate (PR), systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were measured in the supine and standing positions at screening, at study completion and after the different drug administrations. There were no differences in vital signs between the screening and the end-of-study examination in all subjects. Also when the days 1 to 7 of the different study periods and treatment schedules were compared, there were no clinically relevant differences between study groups or periods. Vital signs assessed in the supine and standing positions showed normal diurnal fluctuations.
L4573: 8.2.3. Sponsor's Discussion and Conclusions of Study Results
L4574: Pharmacodynamics
L4575: Co-administration of tyramine increased similarly the systolic blood pressure in all four study groups. Whereas the endpoint was reached at similar tyramine doses for the placebo and 1.0 mg TVP-1012 (rasagiline) groups, it was reached at lower tyramine doses for the 2.0 mg TVP-1012 and the 10 mg selegiline groups.
L4576: The potentiation of tyramine plasma levels is comparable with 2 mg TVP-1012 and 10 mg selegiline, probably due to some peripheral blocking of its degradation.
L4577: Considering the comparability of the effects of 2.0 mg TVP-1012 and 10 mg selegiline, it can be concluded that a daily dose of 2.0 mg TVP-1012 can be administered in further clinical trials without tyramine restrictions.
L4578: Pharmacokinetics
L4579: Definite conclusions on the dose-dependency of the pharmacokinetics of TVP-1012 and its metabolite are difficult to draw due to the small subject number and the administration of only two dose levels (1.0 mg and 2.0 mg TVP-1012). In addition, when the pharmacokinetics were assessed, TVP-1012 was always given together with tyramine. However, it appears that the pharmacokinetics of the parent drug TVP-1012, are dose-dependent with a less than dose-proportional increase in Cmax and a more than dose-proportional increase in AUC. For the metabolite A1, AUC values also increased more than dose-proportionally. Based on previous PK studies it is known that the tmax of rasagiline (PAI) could be 20 minutes. As in this study, the first blood samples were taken as soon as 30 minutes after drug administration, this could explain the lower Cmax as compared to other PK studies.
L4580: Safety
L4581: The tolerability of 1.0 mg and 2.0 mg TVP-1012 was good in the present study. No adverse events clearly attributable to the study medication were observed. The tolerability was comparable to that of placebo or 10 mg selegiline. Minor increases in transaminases (aminotransferases) were of no clinical relevance and resolved spontaneously. There were no particular effects on vital signs, ECG parameters or other laboratory parameters. The most frequent AE observed was palpitation which is frequent with blood pressure enhancing drugs and, therefore, most probably due to tyramine.
L4582: The overall tolerability of TVP-1012 during this study was good and comparable to that of placebo or selegiline. There were no indications to suggest that TVP-1012 causes any clinically significant modification of hemodynamic, electrocardiographic, hematological, biochemical, or clinical parameters.
L4583: The majority of the AEs were experienced after the administration of the higher doses of tyramine and are well-known AEs for systolic blood pressure increasing agents (palpitations). Nearly all other AEs are frequently found in subjects taking part in clinical trials. In addition, none of the AEs was severe or serious in nature.
L4584: There were some slightly out of range values for transaminases activities during the study. However, none of the laboratory tests showed any clinically relevant out of range values at any time-point throughout the study and they normalized spontaneously even under treatment.
L4585: 8.2.4. Reviewer's Comments
L4586: I have several problems/concerns with the design, conduct, and/or analysis of this study and will provide my comments on these various concerns.
L4587: • The achievement of the protocol specified endpoint (i.e. \geq 30 mm Hg systolic blood pressure increment) was based upon a single systolic blood pressure reading collected after the pre-treatment value before tyramine was administered. This is a precarious endpoint because subjects could mount a single increment at that threshold due to an acute stress response. Requiring that the increment occur over a more sustained period such as 3 consecutive increments at or above the specified threshold is a way of trying to decrease the chances of the increment of being a false positive and increasing the chances of the response of being a true positive. This criterion has been used previously by other investigators and is an approach that I strongly endorse.
L4588: The final study report and analyses contained were complicated by mentioning that “clinical criteria” were also applied. However, the second approach for establishing the main study endpoint specifically noted that the protocol specific blood pressure increment was applied AND / OR clinical criteria (4 of which were described in the results section). This description did not say that clinical criteria described were systemically applied but gave the option of using the protocol specified blood pressure increment OR clinical criteria. After much initial confusion and discussion about the application and use of the “clinical criteria,” I have confirmed that clinical criteria were never systemically applied to determining endpoints for all subjects during the conduct of the study (that was completed before the criteria were formally mentioned) nor in the analyses. It appears that the investigator of this study deviated from the protocol in a few instances and gave subjects higher doses of tyramine because he thought the initial 30 mm Hg systolic blood pressure increment was not a true positive response to tyramine. It seemed to me that the sponsor then devised the clinical criteria to try to account for the protocol violations/deviations of the investigator.
L4589: Of interest, the first clinical criterion did not seem logical. This criterion provided that if a subject met the protocol specified systolic blood pressure increment without an “adverse cardiovascular experience” (that was not defined), then the subject should receive a higher dose of tyramine and if the protocol specified blood pressure increment was achieved again, that higher tyramine dose would be recorded as the threshold dose. If this occurred, then I would have expected that the higher tyramine dose would have demonstrated that the initial increment observed was a true positive and thus the lower tyramine dose should have been recorded as the true threshold dose. My view is that attention should be paid only to the strict protocol specified blood pressure increment criterion and that no significant attention should be given to the “clinical criteria.”
L4590: It is also of interest to note that the tyramine threshold data and TSF ratios for individual subjects were not included in the final study report for this study but were contained in a summary document (Appendix 18.2 of the Integrated Summary of Safety - ISS). Furthermore, when these data were presented, the results were noted to be “clinical criteria.” A data listing showing tyramine threshold data and TSF ratios for individual subjects based upon the protocol specified systolic blood pressure increment was only provided by the sponsor following request from DNDP!
L4591: • The sponsor had included calculations of mean TSF when subjects did not experience a protocol specified blood pressure increments and arbitrarily assigned tyramine doses as threshold doses. I do not think that this is advisable and thus have focused on evaluating TSF only when protocol specified blood pressure responses were achieved. Although 27 subjects underwent tyramine testing in both periods, 10 did not achieve a protocol specified blood pressure increment in at least 1 period. The results of the tyramine challenges as reflected by mean TSF (based upon actual protocol specified TYR30 systolic blood pressure increments) show that the 1 mg rasagiline (N = 4) had a similar mean TSF – 1.3 as placebo – 1.1 (N = 5) and did not suggest tyramine potentiation. In contrast, mean TSF for rasagiline was 2.7 (N = 5) and for selegiline was 4.3 (N = 3) and these elevated ratios did suggest some tyramine potentiation. However, the number of subjects per treatment group is extremely limited and does not provide a good representation of what results might be if a much larger sample size had been studied and provided TYR30 threshold doses. This limited result suggests that there is an increase in tyramine sensitivity with the 2 mg rasagiline dose.• I think that it is pertinent to point out that these results were derived from the study of a small number of young males (19-32 years, with average age of 23 – 27 for all groups). It would be highly desirable to assess the effect of rasagiline on a different demographic population consisting of both males and female and also older subjects, particularly considering that most patients using rasagiline are likely to be over 40. I base this comment on both pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic considerations. There are minimal data in which pharmacokinetic parameters of rasagiline were studied in formal PK studies comparing males and females during multidosing and these data showed that rasagiline exposure (i.e. AUC_{last}) was nearly 70 % higher in females. Population PK data also suggest that rasagiline exposure increases by ~ 1 % per year of age. There were
L4592: no formal PK studies of rasagiline to assess the effect of age on PK parameters. Thus, these data suggest that females and older individuals may experience somewhat higher rasagiline exposure. Considering the preliminary findings of this tyramine study that subjects exposed to a higher dose of rasagiline seemed to develop an increase in tyramine sensitivity, it is possible and I would expect that mean TSF for both doses would be higher if larger numbers of subjects were studied and these subjects included females and older individuals up to 70 years. It is also possible that there could be a greater sensitivity to tyramine in elderly/older subjects. I am not aware of any data that have been collected or analyzed that address this issue. Given all these observations, it would be important to study tyramine sensitivity after rasagiline treatment in older (e.g. 40-70 years) males and females.
L4593: • It is relevant to note that the selegiline that was used as a comparator was administered as a single 10 mg dose rather than as 5 mg BID (at morning and lunchtime) according to the U.S. label. I am not aware of data that have shown whether this makes a difference in extent of tyramine potentiation (i.e. TSF). Although 10 mg selegiline (an irreversible selective MAO-B inhibitor) is not generally considered to exhibit any significant MAO-A inhibition, surprisingly there are no published studies that have characterized the TSF when selegiline is dosed BID. Various publications, that are extremely heterogeneous in many study design issues, have shown that swallowed selegiline (10 mg QD - Eldepryl) is associated with a TSF ranging between 2 – 4 in response to oral tyramine administered under fasting conditions. In addition, 2 fasting tyramine studies in NDA 21479 (Zydis selegiline) found a mean TSF of 2.7 and 3.6 for a single dose of 10 mg selegiline. An unpublished tyramine challenge study (while fasting) conducted by the sponsor (Somerset Pharmaceuticals) of selegiline (i.e. Eldepryl) in which selegiline was administered as 5 mg BID showed a TSF of ~ 2. This result, however, contrasts with that of another sponsor (Elan Pharmaceuticals, NDA 21479 for Zydis selegiline) that found that swallowed selegiline (i.e. Eldepryl) administered as 5 mg BID showed a 6.8 mean TSF and this result was similar to the mean TSF result (6.7) for the lowest dose (1.25 mg/day) of Zydis selegiline. Although it is not clear why there might be a somewhat different TSF result for when 10 mg of selegiline is administered as a single dose instead of 2 divided doses, I consider this question to be yet unresolved.
L4594: The mean TSF (based upon tyramine threshold doses associated with actual protocol specified systolic blood pressure increments) was similar for 1 mg/day rasagiline (1.3; N = 4) and for placebo (1.1; N = 5) in the study under review. In contrast, the mean TSF for 2 mg/day rasagiline (2.7; N = 5) and for selegiline (4.3; N = 30) was elevated. These results suggest that there is some tyramine potentiation with the higher dose of rasagiline likely related to some inhibition of MAO-A. The results of only 3-5 subjects per treatment group do not permit an opportunity to observe a variable range of responses. Thus, the extremely small number of subjects in each treatment group do not allow one to draw firm conclusions about the potential for rasagiline to increase the sensitivity to tyramine and the magnitude of the increase for each dose. I consider these results as only very preliminary in suggesting that 1 mg/day rasagiline does not increase tyramine sensitivity and 2 mg/day does increase tyramine sensitivity.
L4595: • In response to my request, the sponsor provided additional analyses of individual subjects for the ratio (Period 2 / Period 1) of their maximal systolic blood pressure responses to all doses of tyramine administered to each treatment group. Mean ratios of each treatment group are shown in Table 16. Mean ratio for 800 mg tyramine was not shown because minimal data were available for these calculations. Whereas the mean ratio of the 1 mg rasagiline group only exceeded all placebo mean ratios at the highest dose of tyramine (400 mg), the mean ratios for 100, 200, and 400 mg tyramine doses in subjects treated with 2 mg rasagiline and 10 mg selegiline were greater than all placebo mean ratios. These result in selegiline and high dose rasagiline groups suggested an effect of treatment consistent with some inhibition of MAO-A. Included in the mean calculations of individual subject ratios were rare, isolated ratios that exceeded 10 in all treatment groups except 1 mg rasagiline. This increased ratio did not seem to be consistently exhibited by the same subject with the exception of subject #617 (2 mg rasagiline group) who showed an increased ratio &gt; 10 for the 100 and 200 mg tyramine challenges (subject # 617 did not have ratios for higher tyramine doses).
